chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Washsha' from Muhammad ibn Humran and Jamil ibn Darraj, both of them from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would, when sending out a raiding party, summon its commander and seat him by his side, and seat his companions in front of him, then say: 'Proceed in the name of Allah and with Allah and in the path of Allah and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). Do not betray, do not be greedy, do not mutilate, and do not cut down a tree unless you are compelled to do so. Do not kill an elder, a child, or a woman. Whoever of the Muslims, whether the lowest or the highest, looks at one of the polytheists, he is a neighbor to him until he hears the word of Allah. If they follow you, then they are your brothers in your religion; and if they refuse, seek help against them from Allah and convey them to their place of safety.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُهَا: The commander of the raiding party
key_terms.تَغُلُّوا: Do not be greedy (specifically regarding hoarding war booty)
key_terms.تُمَثِّلُوا: Do not mutilate (the bodies of the enemy)
key_terms.سَرِيَّةٌ: A military raid or expedition led by a commander under the Prophet's authority
key_terms.مَأْمَنَهُ: Their place of safety or security

ai.seo_question: What are the ethical rules for Muslim military expeditions according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith serves as a foundational legal text for Islamic military jurisprudence, detailing the Prophet’s specific instructions to commanders regarding conduct in war. It establishes the principle of *juran* (temporary protection) for polytheists to facilitate the dissemination of the message, while strictly prohibiting the killing of non-combatants such as women, children, and the elderly, a rule later expanded by Shia scholars to include monks and farmers.
